summary: This informational document covers problems with dynamic DNS when address sharing is used during IPv6 transition, such as with DS-Lite and NAT64. It documents issues and possible solutions, using the Port Control Protocol.

eli5.summary: When many homes share one street address, telling the phone book where you live gets tricky. This RFC explains the trouble and how a port control message can help.

questions: dns update behind shared ipv4 address
how does ddns work with ds-lite
why is address-sharing a problem for ddns
subtitle: How to update DNS when addresses and ports are shared during IPv6 transition.

tldr.problem: Dynamic DNS breaks when multiple devices share a single public IP address (as in DS-Lite and NAT64 during IPv6 transition), because each device gets a different port rather than port 80 or 443, and the DDNS client cannot detect these port changes.
tldr.mechanism: The Port Control Protocol (PCP) can query for external IP addresses and allocated ports, allowing DDNS clients to detect when external ports change and update DNS records with the correct address and port pair.
tldr.outcome: This RFC documents deployment solutions showing how DDNS service providers can support address-sharing scenarios by using PCP information, enabling servers behind CGN devices to remain reachable.

facts.value: MAP request to discover external IP and port

today: RFC 7393 is Informational. It has not been obsoleted. It documents practical solutions for deploying DDNS services in address-sharing networks during IPv6 transition. The approaches described remain applicable for any scenario where devices share public addresses.

sections.title: The Address-Sharing Problem for DDNS
sections.content:
Dynamic DNS (DDNS) is a service that keeps DNS records up to date when a device's IP address changes. It works great when each device has its own public IP address, but breaks down when multiple devices share a single public IP, a scenario called address sharing.

Address sharing happens during IPv6 transition with Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) and NAT64. In these technologies, many customer devices behind a Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) share one public IPv4 address. The CGN assigns each device a unique port number. So instead of reaching a web server at 192.0.2.1:80, visitors must use 192.0.2.1:8001 or 192.0.2.1:8002.

Three problems arise: (1) the DDNS service must register the non-standard port number; (2) the customer's device must create port mappings in the CGN to allow incoming connections; and (3) when the external IP or port changes, the DDNS client must detect this change and update DNS records accordingly.
sections.eli5: In shared-address networks, you can't use the standard port 80—you get an unusual port number like 8001 or 8002. The phone book needs to know your specific port number, not just the street address.

sections.title: Using PCP to Discover and Track Changes
sections.content:
The Port Control Protocol (PCP) is a mechanism for clients to request port mappings from a CGN. PCP allows a client to ask the CGN "What is my external IP address and what port were you assigned to me?" by issuing a PCP MAP request.

The DDNS solution is straightforward: the DDNS client can periodically issue PCP MAP requests to discover its external IP address and port. If either changes from the last known values, the DDNS client sends an update to the DDNS server. PCP handles the technical complexity of figuring out what port the CGN assigned; the DDNS client simply reads the response.

The RFC documents two approaches: (1) the client periodically issues PCP MAP requests with short lifetimes to poll for changes; (2) the client checks a local mapping table maintained by the PCP client and only issues a MAP request if no mapping exists. Both trigger DDNS updates when changes are detected.
sections.eli5: The DDNS client periodically asks the CGN "What's my address and port right now?" If the answer changes, it updates the phone book with the new information.

sections.title: Deployment for Web and Non-Web Services
sections.content:
For web services, the DDNS server learns the external IP and port from the DDNS client and maintains the mapping. When a user visits the DDNS server, it responds with an HTTP 301 redirect pointing to the actual address and port (e.g., 192.0.2.1:8001). The browser follows the redirect to the CGN, which forwards the request to the web server behind it.

For non-web services (FTP, SIP, game servers, etc.), a simple URL redirect does not work. Instead, the DDNS server can host a web portal for each user's registered domain. The portal displays available services with clickable links in various formats (http://, rtsp://, etc.). When a visitor accesses the portal, they see a list of services and their current addresses and ports, allowing them to reach any service.

Both approaches handle the key challenge: mapping between service names and external address/port pairs in a shared-address environment. The DDNS server acts as the rendezvous point, translating domain names to current external coordinates.
sections.eli5: For websites, the phone book redirects visitors to the right apartment number. For other services, the phone book hosts a listing of all available services with their current addresses and ports.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
The RFC does not introduce a new protocol; it describes how to use PCP with existing DDNS services. Security considerations from PCP and DS-Lite apply. DDNS service providers should enforce strong authentication to prevent unauthorized users from modifying records. The proprietary protocols between DDNS client and server may need extensions to support port numbers, which operators should secure.

Denial of Service protection is important: a malicious actor could attempt to flood the DDNS server with bogus updates or DNS hijacking requests. Operators should implement rate limiting, authentication, and request validation. These security concerns are not unique to address-sharing scenarios but apply to all DDNS services.
sections.eli5: DDNS servers need to be careful that only the real owner can update their records, and they need protection against attackers trying to redirect traffic.
